passage:
When the science-fair model collapsed an hour before judging, Hemant's heart hammered. Two classmates were shouting at each other and someone was close to tears. Devika just looked at the pieces, took a breath and said, "Okay. What do we still have?" Her voice was flat.
"She doesn't even care," Hemant muttered to another boy.
Then he noticed her hands sorting screws into a lid, and that she had tied her hair back before anyone spoke. She wasn't indifferent. She was steady. By judging time the model stood, slightly crooked.
Hemant felt ashamed. "Sorry," he told her. "I thought you didn't care."
"I saw all of it," said Devika. "I just didn't want to add to it."

qa.q: What happened an hour before judging?
qa.a: The science-fair model collapsed.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel afterwards about what he said?
qa.a: Ashamed. He realised Devika had been steady, not uncaring, and apologised.

qa.q: What could Hemant do differently the next time a classmate stays composed in a crisis?
qa.a: He could watch what the person does, such as sorting screws and tying back hair, before deciding they don't care, and ask instead of assuming.

qa.q: How does Devika see her own calm?
qa.a: She sees it as a choice not to add to the panic. She noticed all of it but did not want to make it worse.

grounding: Peers see a composed teenager and assume indifference, but the calm is a steady response to a problem she fully sees.

passage:
Jagdish: You didn't even flinch when the coach shouted. Do you care about the team at all?
Ankita: I did care. I heard every word.
Jagdish: You looked bored.
Ankita: I was thinking about what he said, and which part was fair.
Jagdish: I'd have been fuming.
Ankita: I was upset. Inside. But if I'd shouted back, we'd lose the next match too.
Jagdish: Hm. I thought calm meant you didn't mind.
Ankita: It's the opposite. I mind, so I'm not throwing my bag.
Jagdish: Fair. Sorry.
Ankita: Come to practice early? We can fix the passing drill.

qa.q: What did Jagdish accuse Ankita of on the bus stop?
qa.a: Not caring about the team.

qa.q: What did Jagdish believe Ankita's calm meant?
qa.a: Jagdish believed calm meant Ankita did not mind, until Ankita explained about being upset inside.

qa.q: What could Jagdish and Ankita do next, according to Ankita?
qa.a: Come to practice early and fix the passing drill together.

qa.q: How does Ankita feel about the coach's shouting?
qa.a: Upset inside, but Ankita chooses not to shout back, because it could cost the next match too.

grounding: Peers see a composed teenager and assume indifference, but real calm notices the problem and chooses not to be thrown.

passage:
In Class 10, when our team's science project collapsed the night before the exhibition, everyone panicked. Ritesh shouted at the printer, Lopa cried in the corridor, and I kept refreshing the group chat. Urmila just sat on the floor with the broken model and started sorting pieces.
I was annoyed. "Do you even care?" I snapped at her.
She looked up and said evenly, "I care a lot. That's why I'm not wasting time panicking." Then she listed what we could still save: the poster, the working motor and a simpler demo.
We didn't win, but we presented something. I remember thinking her calm was coldness. It wasn't. She'd seen the problem more clearly than any of us. I'm Divyansh, and I still think of her when I start flapping.

qa.q: What three things did Urmila say they could still save?
qa.a: The poster, the working motor and a simpler demo.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when snapping "Do you even care?"
qa.a: Divyansh felt annoyed and panicked, mistaking Urmila's calm for not caring.

qa.q: How can someone tell calm from not caring?
qa.a: Calm still sees the problem fully and acts on it, as Urmila did by listing what could be saved; indifference would do nothing.

qa.q: How might Urmila have felt being accused of not caring?
qa.a: Urmila was probably a little hurt, but stayed steady and explained she cared a lot.

grounding: Shows a peer mistaking a composed teenager's calm for not caring, then seeing it was clear-sighted serenity.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 11, Wednesday.
Several students complained that Jyoti "doesn't care" about the debate final, because she stayed calm while the team argued about losing their lead speaker to illness. Some called her cold.
I watched her at practice today. She listened to every worry, wrote them all down, then said evenly, "Okay. I'll take the opening. Arjun takes rebuttal. We rehearse at lunch." When a teammate accused her of not caring, she said, "I care. I'm just not going to panic."
Later she told me she hadn't slept well from nerves. The calm was a choice, not an absence of feeling.
Next step: talk to the team about the difference between calm and indifference.
Ramesh

qa.q: Which part did Jyoti say she would take?
qa.a: The opening.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling underneath her calm?
qa.a: Jyoti was nervous, enough to sleep badly, but chose not to panic.

qa.q: What does Ramesh plan, and why?
qa.a: To talk to the team about calm versus indifference, since they misread Jyoti's composure as not caring.

qa.q: How did some teammates see Jyoti's calm?
qa.a: They saw it as cold, as if she didn't care about the final.

grounding: Shows peers taking a composed teenager's calm for not caring, while an observer sees it is chosen steadiness.

passage:
Monday
Today the water pipe burst in the hostel and flooded half our floor. Everyone was screaming and grabbing their books. Elizabeth, from the room next to mine, just stood there for a second, then calmly unplugged the extension cords, moved her laptop up high, and went to find the warden.
I honestly thought, wow, she doesn't care at all. Her books were soaked and she didn't even cry.
Later I saw her sitting on the stairs, drying pages one by one with a hairdryer, hands a bit shaky. She said, "I'm upset. I just knew the wires were the dangerous part."
I felt bad for judging her. She'd noticed more than any of us.
Vandana

qa.q: What did Elizabeth unplug?
qa.a: The extension cords.

qa.q: What did Vandana first think about Elizabeth's calm, and how did that change?
qa.a: Vandana first thought Elizabeth didn't care, then felt bad for judging after seeing the shaky hands on the stairs.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth's calm allow her to do?
qa.a: It let her notice the real danger, the wires, unplug them and fetch the warden while others panicked.

qa.q: How was Elizabeth feeling on the stairs?
qa.a: Elizabeth was upset, hands a bit shaky, drying soaked pages one by one.

grounding: Shows an observer mistaking a composed peer's calm for indifference, then seeing she had noticed the problem fully.
